description: The maintainer's adjacency ruling on issue #944's sibling question: a newline separates exactly like a space -- always, everywhere. Adjacency is whitespace-agnostic; a newline is insignificant to the GRAMMAR, not invisible to the LEXER, and it is now written down normatively at `spec/grammar.md:248`. This is a NARROWING, and the mechanism is why it was invisible: a newline token's `end` IS the next line's column 1, so once a container skipped the newline the following `[` tested as adjacent to what preceded it -- a skipped newline MANUFACTURED an adjacency the source never had. Measured against the built parser at `0277d5ff` before the fix, `[ :nums` + newline + `[1] ]` read `[1]` as a SELECTOR on `:nums` and printed `[10]`, while the spaced `[ :nums [1] ]` read a second element and printed `[[10 20 30] [1]]`. The two spellings now agree, and this fixture proves it as a VALUE rather than as a diagnostic, which is why a list literal is the container: both spellings execute in it. The parenthesized container is malformed in BOTH spellings, so its agreement is pinned in the companion `core-language/check/a-newline-separates-like-a-space-when-malformed`; the top level is excluded from both, because its spaced spelling is an arity error unrelated to adjacency. The glued spelling is printed too and must NOT match the other two: without it this fixture would still pass if adjacency stopped working altogether, since all three spellings would then agree on the non-selector reading. The final row is the one-line comprehension, which still maps rather than indexing `:nums`; its SPLIT form is a parse error and so lives in the check twin.
